chapter: Newark and first years in Harlem
title: The crash, Lenox Club and Jack Johnson
summary: After Wall Street crashed Butler took a job in Cliff Jackson's band at the Lenox Club and recalls Fowler's band stranded in Shenandoah, Jack Johnson as band owner and Johnson's advice about using one's head.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Well, we were making $50.00. You know, that was good. Some of them big fellows, they were making $150.00, like Fletcher was paying $150.00 then, you know. These cats (inaudible). But we were supposed to go in there and Wall Street crashed. I just remember Wall Street crashing and everything went to pot. Everything, big bands, music was cut out, and at that time there were speakeasies and all these things, too. So it was very, very, very difficult. Very difficult. Then I got a job working with this man, Cliff Jackson, as I told you, playing trumpet at a place called the Lenox Club. Now, the Lenox Club was a place where the people who couldn't go to the Cotton Club, because the Cotton Club didn't really allow people of color in there, although those chorus girls and all were those beautiful people of color. You had a problem getting in there. And first it was Jack Johnson's Club. But firstly, in Billy Fowler's band, Jack Johnson had the band. And Billy Fowler was conducting. So we got stranded down there in Shenandoah, Pennsylvania, at Tommy Dorsey's home. We got stranded there in two ways, we got snowed in and we didn't get paid. But Jack Johnson was working for this German man. And that's the last time I saw Jack
So, the Cotton Club didn't allow --
Had you seen him many times before that?

I seen him, because he lived up the street from me. I seen him many times. And he was talking so about boxing. And one man asked him, well, what do you think? He said, 'Don't let nobody get to your head, son. Use your head, don't let nobody use it for you.'
